title: Gaps and Islands
description: Group consecutive values into ranges with a row-number difference trick.

data.text: A `LoginDays` table stores the distinct dates each user was active. For every user, return each **continuous streak of consecutive dates** as a single row with a start and end date, plus the length in days. Do it in one query without a cursor or recursive CTE.

data.title: SQL Solution
data.code:
-- Key idea: within a run of consecutive dates, (date - row_number) is constant.
WITH Numbered AS
(
    SELECT
        UserId,
        LoginDate,
        ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY UserId ORDER BY LoginDate) AS rn
    FROM LoginDays
),
Grouped AS
(
    SELECT
        UserId,
        LoginDate,
        DATEADD(day, -rn, LoginDate) AS IslandKey   -- constant inside a streak
    FROM Numbered
)
SELECT
    UserId,
    MIN(LoginDate)                                  AS StreakStart,
    MAX(LoginDate)                                  AS StreakEnd,
    DATEDIFF(day, MIN(LoginDate), MAX(LoginDate)) + 1 AS StreakDays
FROM Grouped
GROUP BY UserId, IslandKey
ORDER BY UserId, StreakStart;

data.title: Explanation
data.text: The trick is that subtracting a **dense sequential row number** from the value itself collapses each consecutive run to a single constant. For dates 2024-01-01, 02, 03 the differences are the same, but a gap (01, 02, 05) produces two distinct constants — so `GROUP BY` on that constant, with `MIN`/`MAX`, gives you the islands. To find the **gaps** instead, take each island's `StreakEnd`, add one day via `LEAD`, and report the interval to the next `StreakStart`. The same pattern solves consecutive sequence numbers, contiguous ID ranges, and version runs — anywhere you need to convert "consecutive values" into "ranges".
